triage.name: GERD
triage.reason: Very common reflux presentation with classic heartburn history and response to therapy; good ambulatory case with alarm-feature reasoning.

review_issues: auto-repaired: labs: dropped 'cbc' (not in the reference table)

demographics: More common in people with obesity

risk_factors.text: Cigarette smoking or secondhand smoke exposure

family_history: GERD or frequent heartburn in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: I get a burning feeling in my chest after I eat
Sour liquid comes up into my throat
It gets worse when I lie down at night

hpi.onset: Gradual, often over weeks to months; many patients have had intermittent symptoms for years
hpi.duration: Chronic, typically present for months to years
hpi.progression: Symptoms come and go, often worse after large meals or when lying down; may slowly increase in frequency over time
hpi.location: Burning behind the breastbone (mid-chest), sometimes rising into the throat
hpi.radiation: Can radiate upward toward the throat or neck; occasionally to the back
hpi.quality: Burning or warm, sometimes sour or acid-like
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually 3–6/10, worse after meals
hpi.timing: Typically 30–60 minutes after meals and when lying down or bending over
aggravating: Lying down or bending over soon after eating
Spicy foods, chocolate, caffeine, citrus, tomato
relieving: Elevating the head of the bed

associated_symptoms.text: Regurgitation of sour or bitter fluid
Hoarse or raspy voice, especially in the morning
Sensation of a lump in the throat

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain with shortness of breath, sweating, or pain radiating to the jaw or arm
Choking or coughing up food at night

argues_against: Pneumonia or other acute lung infection

atypical.how_it_differs: Older children may report heartburn, but younger children often present with recurrent vomiting, poor feeding, irritability, or respiratory symptoms rather than classic burning chest pain.
missing_classic_features: Clear relationship to meals and lying down

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants typically present with spitting up, feeding refusal, arching of the back, irritability, or poor weight gain; classic heartburn cannot be reported.
missing_classic_features: Regurgitation described as sour or acid

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be milder or atypical, with more dysphagia, respiratory symptoms, or silent reflux; they are also more likely to have severe esophagitis or Barrett's esophagus.
Heartburn is very common in the third trimester due to increased abdominal pressure and hormonal effects; symptoms usually improve after delivery.
Symptoms tend to be more frequent and severe, and are more likely to persist; weight loss often improves symptoms.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort, occasionally clears throat or shifts position for reflux symptoms
general.severe: Uncomfortable, frequent throat clearing or cough, appears fatigued from nocturnal symptoms
general.critical: Ill-appearing with signs of GI bleeding (pallor, diaphoresis) or severe pain suggesting complication

findings.finding: Mild epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants and check for organomegaly
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without masses or organomegaly

findings.maneuver: Perform Murphy sign (press under the right costal margin while the patient inhales)
findings.finding: No arrest of inspiration or right upper quadrant tenderness

findings.maneuver: Check for rebound tenderness and involuntary guarding
Inspect the posterior pharynx and oropharynx
findings.finding: Erythema or erosions on the posterior pharyngeal wall or uvula

findings.maneuver: Inspect the teeth for enamel erosion
findings.finding: Loss of enamel on the lingual surfaces of teeth

findings.maneuver: Listen to the patient's voice during history

findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate peripheral pulses
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, no jugular venous distension or peripheral edema

findings.maneuver: Palpate the anterior chest wall and reproduce any chest pain
Palpate the cervical, supraclavicular, and axillary lymph nodes
findings.finding: No enlarged or tender lymph nodes

labs.caveat: Anemia is not caused by uncomplicated GERD; when present it points to erosive esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, or a separate bleeding lesion.
Low ferritin supports chronic blood loss from esophagitis rather than GERD itself.
Negative. Check in anyone who could be pregnant before endoscopy, sedation, or reflux medications that are not pregnancy-safe.
Normal. Must be checked when chest pain could be cardiac; a normal troponin helps exclude acute coronary syndrome before attributing pain to reflux.
Normal. Useful when epigastric pain raises concern for pancreatitis rather than reflux.

findings.finding: No ST elevation or depression; no ischemic changes
Normal PR and QRS intervals without block

imaging.preferred_when: Alarm features, age over 60 with new symptoms, or failure of empiric therapy

findings.text: Erythema, friability, or linear erosions in the distal esophagus (erosive esophagitis)
Mucosal breaks or ulceration in severe esophagitis
Salmon-colored tongues of mucosa extending above the gastroesophageal junction (Barrett's esophagus)

imaging.preferred_when: Dysphagia or suspected stricture when endoscopy is not immediately available

findings.text: Free reflux of contrast from stomach into esophagus
Smooth tapering stricture in the distal esophagus

imaging.preferred_when: Normal endoscopy with persistent symptoms, or before antireflux surgery

findings.text: Increased esophageal acid exposure time (pH below 4 for more than about 4–6% of the study)
Symptom episodes correlate with acid reflux events

imaging.preferred_when: Before antireflux surgery or when a motility disorder is suspected

findings.text: Low lower esophageal sphincter resting pressure
Weak or absent peristalsis suggesting a motility disorder
Usually normal; no role in diagnosing GERD
Retrocardiac air-fluid level from a large hiatal hernia

initial.why: Baseline blood count; anemia would suggest erosive disease or another bleeding source
initial.only_if: alarm features such as dysphagia, weight loss, or suspected GI bleeding

initial.why: Excludes acute coronary syndrome when chest pain could be cardiac
initial.only_if: chest pain is not clearly reflux, or there are cardiac risk factors

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before endoscopy, sedation, or medication changes
Directly assesses for esophagitis, stricture, and Barrett's esophagus
initial.only_if: alarm features, age over 60 with new symptoms, or failure of empiric PPI therapy

confirmatory.why: Documents abnormal acid exposure when symptoms persist despite therapy and endoscopy is normal

supporting.why: Evaluates anatomy and stricture when endoscopy is unavailable or not tolerated
Assesses peristalsis and sphincter function before antireflux surgery
supporting.only_if: antireflux surgery is being considered or a motility disorder is suspected

supporting.why: Excludes pancreatitis when epigastric pain is prominent

not_indicated.why: Does not diagnose GERD and rarely changes management
No role in typical reflux symptoms
Not useful for reflux; consider only if biliary or pancreatic disease is suspected

decision_points: Trial of lifestyle changes plus a proton pump inhibitor is appropriate first-line therapy for classic symptoms without alarm features
Endoscopy is indicated for alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, anemia), age over 60 with new-onset symptoms, or failure of empiric therapy
Exclude cardiac causes of chest pain before attributing symptoms to GERD when the presentation is atypical
pH monitoring is reserved for persistent symptoms with normal endoscopy or before antireflux surgery

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Burning mid-chest discomfort that can be mistaken for heartburn; both are common and can occur after meals or at rest
differential.trigger: Chest pain with exertional onset, diaphoresis, shortness of breath, or pain radiating to the jaw, neck, or arm

history: Pressure or squeezing quality rather than burning
Provoked by exertion and relieved by rest
Radiation to jaw, neck, or left arm
Associated dyspnea, diaphoresis, or nausea
Cardiac risk factors such as diabetes, smoking, hypertension, or hyperlipidemia
imaging: Regional wall motion abnormality on echocardiography
ecg: New Q waves or conduction abnormality

differential.name: Peptic ulcer disease
differential.why_considered: Epigastric burning pain that may be relieved or worsened by food and overlaps with reflux symptoms
differential.trigger: Epigastric pain that wakes the patient at night, or melena, hematemesis, or anemia

history: Epigastric rather than retrosternal pain
Pain relieved by food (duodenal) or worsened by food (gastric)
NSAID use or prior H. pylori infection
Melena or hematemesis
exam: Signs of anemia such as pallor
labs: Positive H. pylori stool antigen or urea breath test
imaging: Gastric or duodenal ulcer on endoscopy
Free air on upright chest x-ray if perforated

differential.name: Esophageal cancer
differential.why_considered: Reflux is a risk factor and early disease can present with heartburn or regurgitation before dysphagia develops
differential.trigger: Progressive solid-food dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, or iron-deficiency anemia in a patient with long-standing reflux

history: Progressive dysphagia, first to solids then liquids
Unintentional weight loss
Odynophagia
Long-standing GERD or Barrett's esophagus
Tobacco or heavy alcohol use
labs: Elevated liver enzymes if hepatic metastases
imaging: Irregular mass or stricture with mucosal destruction on endoscopy
Mass or lymphadenopathy on CT or endoscopic ultrasound

differential.name: Achalasia
differential.why_considered: Regurgitation and chest discomfort that can be mistaken for reflux

history: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset
Regurgitation of undigested food hours after eating
Nocturnal regurgitation and aspiration
Heartburn less prominent or absent
imaging: Dilated esophagus with a smooth bird-beak narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction on barium swallow
Absent peristalsis and failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation on manometry

differential.name: Functional heartburn
differential.why_considered: Burning retrosternal discomfort with normal endoscopy and no response to acid suppression

history: Symptoms persist despite adequate proton pump inhibitor therapy
No relationship to meals or lying down
Associated anxiety or somatization
labs: Normal blood count and metabolic panel
imaging: Normal esophageal acid exposure on pH monitoring
No symptom correlation with reflux events

differential.name: Eosinophilic esophagitis
differential.why_considered: Reflux-like symptoms with dysphagia, more common in younger patients with atopy

history: Dysphagia or food impaction
History of asthma, eczema, or allergic rhinitis
Poor response to proton pump inhibitors
exam: Oral allergy findings such as lip or tongue swelling
imaging: Rings, furrows, or white exudates on endoscopy

differential.name: Biliary colic or cholecystitis
differential.why_considered: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain after fatty meals that can be confused with reflux

history: Pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium
Colicky pain after fatty meals
Radiation to the right shoulder or back
Fever and vomiting if cholecystitis
exam: Right upper quadrant tenderness or palpable gallbladder
labs: Elevated alkaline phosphatase, GGT, or bilirubin
imaging: Gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, or pericholecystic fluid on ultrasound
Biliary dilation on ultrasound or MRCP

severity.mild: Intermittent heartburn less than twice a week, no nocturnal symptoms, no esophagitis on endoscopy, symptoms controlled with lifestyle changes or occasional antacids
severity.moderate: Heartburn two or more times a week, nocturnal symptoms, mild erosive esophagitis (Los Angeles grade A or B), symptoms controlled with daily proton pump inhibitor
severity.severe: Daily symptoms despite proton pump inhibitor, severe erosive esophagitis (grade C or D), peptic stricture, or Barrett's esophagus
severity.critical: Complicated disease with GI bleeding, perforation, or severe aspiration; life-threatening but uncommon

red_flags.meaning: Suggests stricture, severe esophagitis, or malignancy; endoscopy is indicated
Raises concern for malignancy or severe dysphagia; endoscopy is indicated
Suggests erosive esophagitis, ulcer, or malignancy; urgent endoscopy is indicated

red_flags.finding: Chest pain with dyspnea, diaphoresis, or radiation to jaw or arm
red_flags.meaning: Must exclude acute coronary syndrome before attributing to reflux
Suggests severe reflux with aspiration risk; further evaluation and aggressive therapy needed

red_flags.finding: Failure of an adequate proton pump inhibitor trial
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an alternative diagnosis or complicated disease; endoscopy and pH monitoring should be considered

complications.name: Peptic stricture
clues: Smooth tapering narrowing on barium swallow

complications.name: Barrett's esophagus
clues: Salmon-colored mucosa above the gastroesophageal junction on endoscopy

complications.name: Esophageal adenocarcinoma
clues: Irregular mass or malignant stricture on endoscopy

special_populations.differences: Older children may report heartburn, but younger children often present with recurrent vomiting, poor feeding, irritability, or respiratory symptoms rather than classic burning chest pain.
Infants typically present with spitting up, feeding refusal, arching of the back, irritability, or poor weight gain; classic heartburn cannot be reported.
Symptoms may be milder or atypical, with more dysphagia, respiratory symptoms, or silent reflux; they are also more likely to have severe esophagitis or Barrett's esophagus.

Heartburn is very common in the third trimester due to increased abdominal pressure and hormonal effects; symptoms usually improve after delivery. Treatment options are limited to pregnancy-safe medications.
Symptoms tend to be more frequent and severe, and are more likely to persist; weight loss often improves symptoms.

key_questions.question: What does the burning feel like, and where exactly is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Burning behind the breastbone (mid-chest), sometimes rising into the throat

key_questions.question: When does it happen in relation to meals and lying down?
key_questions.looking_for: 30–60 minutes after meals, worse when lying down or bending over

key_questions.question: How often do you get it, and how long has this been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Two or more times a week for months to years supports GERD rather than occasional reflux

key_questions.question: Does anything come up into your throat or mouth?
key_questions.looking_for: Regurgitation of sour or bitter fluid, or a sudden excess of saliva (water brash)

key_questions.question: What makes it better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with large, fatty, or spicy meals, alcohol, caffeine, chocolate, and tight clothing; better with antacids and sitting upright

key_questions.question: Do you have any trouble swallowing, painful swallowing, or food getting stuck?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive solid-food dysphagia or odynophagia suggests stricture, severe esophagitis, or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you vomited blood or coffee-ground material, or had black tarry stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Hematemesis or melena suggests erosive esophagitis, ulcer, or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss raises concern for malignancy or severe dysphagia

key_questions.question: Does the chest pain ever come with shortness of breath, sweating, or pain in your jaw or arm?
key_questions.looking_for: These features suggest acute coronary syndrome and must be excluded before attributing pain to reflux

key_questions.question: Do you have a chronic cough, hoarse voice, or a lump-in-the-throat feeling?
key_questions.looking_for: Extraesophageal reflux symptoms such as dry cough, morning hoarseness, or globus

key_questions.question: Do you ever wake at night with reflux, cough, or choking?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturnal symptoms suggest more severe disease and aspiration risk

key_questions.question: What medicines do you take, including over-the-counter pain relievers?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs, aspirin, alendronate, calcium channel blockers, nitrates, or prednisone can worsen reflux

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or drink alcohol, and how much?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco and alcohol use are modifiable risk factors

key_questions.question: Have you gained weight recently, or do you eat large or late meals?
key_questions.looking_for: Obesity and late evening meals are strong contributors to reflux

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had frequent heartburn or GERD?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of GERD or frequent heartburn

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy is a common cause of reflux and affects medication and testing choices

reasoning_points: Classic burning retrosternal discomfort occurring 30–60 minutes after meals and worse when lying down or bending over
Regurgitation of sour or bitter fluid, sometimes with water brash
Symptoms occurring two or more times a week over months to years, distinguishing GERD from occasional physiologic reflux
Relief with antacids and with sitting upright, and improvement with smaller meals and head-of-bed elevation
Risk factors such as obesity, hiatal hernia, smoking, pregnancy, and large or late meals
No alarm features: no dysphagia, odynophagia, GI bleeding, anemia, or unintentional weight loss
Cardiac causes of chest pain excluded when the presentation is atypical
Extraesophageal symptoms such as chronic dry cough, hoarseness, or globus sensation support the diagnosis
Diagnosis is clinical in typical cases; endoscopy is reserved for alarm features, older age with new symptoms, or failure of empiric therapy

easy: Middle-aged adult with classic postprandial burning behind the breastbone
Symptoms worse lying down and relieved by antacids
Obesity or known hiatal hernia as a risk factor
No alarm features and a normal abdominal and cardiac exam
medium: Predominant extraesophageal symptoms such as chronic dry cough or morning hoarseness without much heartburn
Chest pain that requires excluding acute coronary syndrome before attributing it to reflux
Pregnancy with third-trimester heartburn and limited medication options
Symptoms that persist despite lifestyle changes and require a proton pump inhibitor trial
hard: Older adult with new-onset symptoms and mild or atypical complaints, raising concern for complicated disease
Long-standing reflux with progressive dysphagia suggesting a peptic stricture or malignancy
Normal endoscopy with persistent symptoms, requiring pH monitoring to distinguish GERD from functional heartburn
Overlap with peptic ulcer disease, biliary colic, or eosinophilic esophagitis in a younger patient with atopy
